item.title: Gold's downside looks limited because the dollar has already done most of its work, CBA says
item.description:
If CBA is right, gold traders should be watching the dollar index and US real yields more closely than geopolitical headlines. The December Fed decision is the near-term test. A hike that is already expected, with no hawkish surprise in the guidance, could let the dollar plateau and help gold stabilise. A signal that more hikes are coming would push real yields higher and test the lower end of CBA's range. Gold's renewed inverse link to the dollar also means moves in dollar-yen and euro-dollar may give an early read on bullion. With only weeks until year-end, CBA's range doubles as a near-term trading band.

---

Earlier:

  • HSBC flags $3,400 as gold's next big test and says it is too early to call a bottom
  • Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test

---

CBA says gold has gone back to trading off the dollar and real yields rather than haven demand, and with the dollar already close to the bank's forecast peak, it sees limited downside and a year-end range of $3,500 to $3,700.

Summary:

  • CBA expects gold at around $3,500 to $3,700 an ounce at year-end
  • The bank says the dollar's trajectory will be a key driver of gold prices in the coming months
  • "Sell America" and dollar-debasement trades are giving way to gold's traditional inverse links with the dollar and US real yields
  • Structural safe-haven demand has become a less important support for gold
  • The dollar has risen faster than CBA expected and is near the peak it forecast for mid-2027, suggesting limited downside for gold

The dollar is set to be the main force behind gold prices in the coming months, according to Commonwealth Bank of Australia. The bank argues that the downside for the metal now looks limited, because the greenback is already close to its expected peak.

CBA expects gold to end the year at around $3,500 to $3,700 an ounce, close to where the metal has been trading this week after a steep selloff. The bank's case rests on a shift in what is driving bullion. Earlier in the cycle, the "sell America" trade and bets on a weakening, debased dollar pushed investors towards gold as a structural haven. Those trades are now giving way to more traditional relationships, CBA said, in particular gold's tendency to move in the opposite direction to the dollar and to US 10-year real Treasury yields. As a result, structural safe-haven demand has become a less important support for the metal.

That puts the dollar's trajectory at the centre of the outlook. The greenback has risen faster than CBA expected and is now close to the peak the bank had forecast for the middle of 2027. If most of the dollar's rally is already done, the main headwind for gold may be close to its maximum strength. In CBA's view, that suggests the risk of further steep losses in gold is limited.

The call fits the broader picture of gold's slide this year. The metal has fallen sharply as a stronger dollar, rising expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes and selling in stock markets pushed investors to raise cash. Higher real yields increase the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and that relationship appears to be reasserting itself.

CBA's view sits at the more constructive end of a divided field. HSBC warned this week that continued equity weakness could push gold through major support at $3,400, and said it is too early to call an end to the slide. Saxo's Ole Hansen, by contrast, pointed to signs of selling exhaustion and set out a path towards around $3,700 if gold can close above roughly $3,590.

The risks to CBA's view run through the same channel. A dollar that overshoots the bank's forecast peak, or a further rise in real yields if the Fed hikes more aggressively than expected, would leave gold vulnerable. On the other hand, any sign that the dollar has topped out would strengthen the case that the worst of gold's decline is over.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Kiwi edges higher as official NZ election count confirms a hung parliament
item.description:
The muted reaction suggests NZD traders are pricing politics as noise unless talks break down. The tail risk is a failed negotiation and a fresh election, which would bring a longer period of uncertainty and could weigh on the currency and New Zealand government bonds. Coalition deals that come with large fiscal commitments are the other thing to watch, especially for bond yields. Outside Wellington, the kiwi remains tied to global risk sentiment and the US dollar. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December and AI-related volatility still unsettling equities, those forces are likely to outweigh the election result.

---

---

New Zealand's official count has confirmed a hung parliament, but the kiwi's small rise suggests currency traders see coalition talks as a political puzzle rather than an economic threat, at least for now.

Summary:

  • The New Zealand dollar edged higher after official election results confirmed a hung parliament
  • The incumbent centre-right coalition will need the centrist Opportunity Party to govern
  • The small move suggests markets see limited immediate economic risk from coalition talks
  • A prolonged stalemate or a fresh election remains the main political risk for the currency
  • Global risk appetite, the US dollar and the RBNZ outlook are likely to remain the bigger drivers

The New Zealand dollar edged higher on Friday after official election results confirmed a hung parliament. The modest move suggests currency traders see little immediate economic risk in the drawn-out coalition talks that now lie ahead.

The final count from the Electoral Commission left the incumbent centre-right coalition short of a majority on its own, so it will need the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to govern. The result removes some of the uncertainty that hung over the preliminary election-night tally, even if it doesn't yet settle who will form the next government.

The kiwi's gain of a few points was small by any measure, and the lack of a sharper reaction is telling. Political uncertainty in New Zealand rarely moves the currency for long, and markets appear to be treating the result as a question of coalition arithmetic rather than a shift in economic direction. Having a centrist kingmaker, rather than a party on either ideological flank, may also limit concern about abrupt changes to fiscal policy.

The risks haven't disappeared. Negotiations could stretch on for weeks, and if no workable government emerges, New Zealand could face a fresh election. A prolonged stalemate, or a deal that came with significant spending or tax commitments, could test the currency and the local bond market. For now, though, traders seem content to wait.

In the meantime, the kiwi's direction is likely to depend on more familiar drivers. Global risk appetite has been fragile amid turmoil in AI-linked stocks, and the New Zealand dollar, like its Australian counterpart, tends to struggle when investors retreat from risk. The US dollar has been supported by expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Moves in those markets, along with the outlook for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, are likely to matter more for the kiwi in the coming days than developments in Wellington.

Traders will watch for any signs of progress in coalition talks, but unless the politics turn messy, the election looks set to remain a sideshow for the currency. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tokyo core inflation hits 16-month high of 2.9%, firming the case for a December BoJ hike
item.description:
The data keeps a December hike as the base case, which should limit any yen weakness. With the yen near 160 per dollar, however, a 25 basis point move that is already widely expected may do little on its own. The bigger driver for the currency is likely to be any signal that the BoJ will speed up its pace of hikes, as board member Naoki Tamura has urged. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields remain sensitive to that guidance. Stock market instability tied to AI and chips is the main risk to the hike call, so a sharp drop in Japanese equities would quickly cut the odds of a December move.

---

Data post here earlier:

  • Tokyo November core CPI rises to 2.9% y/y, just shy of 3.0% expected

---

Tokyo core inflation has climbed to its fastest pace in 16 months, strengthening the case for a December BoJ hike, though a slight easing in the bank's preferred trend gauge suggests energy did much of the lifting.

Summary:

  • Tokyo core CPI rose 2.9% y/y in November, the fastest pace since July 2025, up from 2.6% but just below the 3.0% forecast
  • Core inflation has stayed above the BoJ's 2% target for three straight months
  • The end of utility subsidies contributed, but price rises were broad-based, including food, daily necessities and hotel charges
  • The measure excluding fresh food and energy eased to 2.5% from 2.6%
  • Markets expect the BoJ to raise rates to 1.5% at its December 17-18 meeting, with a Reuters poll majority also seeing another hike by end-March
  • Board member Naoki Tamura called for swift action against an inflation overshoot, including faster hikes

Core inflation in Tokyo climbed to its highest in 16 months in November, keeping price growth well above the Bank of Japan's 2% target and reinforcing expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates next month.

Core consumer prices in the capital, which include fuel but exclude fresh food, rose 2.9% from a year earlier, according to data reported by Reuters on Friday. That was up from 2.6% in October and the fastest annual pace since July 2025, although it fell just short of the 3.0% median forecast. Core inflation has now held above the BoJ's target for three consecutive months.

The end of government utility subsidies accounted for part of the jump, but the increases were broad-based, with prices rising for food, daily necessities and hotel stays. One economist expects core inflation to keep accelerating as higher energy costs from the Middle East conflict feed through into other prices.

The picture is a little softer underneath. A measure that strips out both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches closely as a gauge of trend inflation, eased slightly to 2.5% from 2.6% in October. That leaves underlying inflation comfortably above target, but suggests energy did much of the heavy lifting in the core rise.

Tokyo figures are widely seen as a leading indicator for the nationwide data. Those are due on the morning of December 18 in Tokyo, the final day of the BoJ's two-day policy meeting. That timing makes Friday's release one of the last major inflation readings that policymakers and markets can fully weigh before the decision.

Markets widely expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5% from 1.25% at that meeting. The bank has already moved faster than in previous years, hiking in June and again in September, compared with roughly two hikes a year in 2024 and 2025. In October it held rates, but said underlying inflation had roughly reached its 2% target and signalled readiness to keep tightening. A majority of economists in a Reuters poll expect a December hike followed by another by the end of March, with many seeing rates peaking at around 1.75% or 2.0%.

Hawkish board member Naoki Tamura added to the pressure on Thursday, saying the bank must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by speeding up its pace of hikes.

The main risk to a December move comes from markets. The same economist said the BoJ could hold off if instability linked to worries over AI and the chip sector persists, though a hike next month remains the baseline.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: HSBC flags $3,400 as gold's next big test and says it is too early to call a bottom
item.description:
Gold is trading as a risk asset rather than a haven, so equity markets have become the key driver. Another leg lower in stocks would raise the chance of a test of $3,400, while a stabilisation would ease the forced selling. Silver and platinum group metals face an extra layer of risk from tariffs that could hit the industries using them, even though HSBC still expects silver to be in deficit. US tariff announcements are worth watching, especially any aimed at Mexico or Canada, which HSBC sees as the exception that could lift silver. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December, a softer turn in US data is the most likely trigger for relief.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test

---

HSBC sees gold's fortunes tied to a weak stock market, with $3,400 the next major support at risk, and warns that proposed tariffs could hurt silver and platinum group metals more than gold itself.

Summary:

  • HSBC warns continued equity market weakness puts gold at risk of breaking its next major support at $3,400 an ounce
  • The bank says it is too early to call a halt to gold's slide, though the selloff may have limits
  • Trade distortions are traditionally positive for gold, but proposed tariffs could hit silver- and PGM-intensive industries
  • HSBC still projects a silver deficit this year despite declines in high-tech and industrial demand
  • It does not expect fresh tariffs alone to lift silver unless they target Mexico and Canada

HSBC says it is too early to call an end to gold's slide, warning that further weakness in stock markets could push the metal through its next major support at $3,400 an ounce. The bank also sees limits to how far the selloff can run.

The warning, carried by Reuters on Thursday, adds to the cautious camp as gold struggles to find a floor. HSBC's chief precious metals analyst, James Steel, tied the risk directly to equities. Gold traded near $3,570 on Thursday in thin holiday conditions, after slipping below $3,500 midweek to its lowest in more than a year. The link to stocks reflects the forced selling behind the metal's fall this year: investors raising cash to cover equity losses have been selling what they can, including gold.

The $3,400 level carries extra weight in Steel's analysis. He has previously described it as roughly the inflation-adjusted equivalent of gold's old record high, a level the metal broke above in 2025. A sustained move back below it would undo a milestone that helped define gold's bull run.

HSBC also turned to trade policy. Trade distortions have traditionally been positive for gold, the bank said, but proposed new US tariffs could weigh on industries that use large amounts of silver and platinum group metals. That puts the industrial side of the precious metals complex more at risk than gold itself.

On silver, HSBC still projects a market deficit this year, even as demand from high-tech and industrial users declines. It does not expect fresh tariffs on their own to push silver prices higher, unless they are aimed at Mexico and Canada, both important suppliers of silver to the US.

HSBC's view adds to a growing debate over whether gold has bottomed. TD Securities' head of commodity strategy also said on Thursday that it is likely too early to call a low in gold and the wider precious metals complex. Others see the selloff as overdone. Saxo's Ole Hansen pointed this week to signs of selling exhaustion, stretched positioning and a strong seasonal record over December and January. He stressed, though, that a lasting recovery depends on the dollar and rate expectations easing.

For now, markets are pricing a high chance of another Federal Reserve rate hike in December, which continues to weigh on a metal that pays no yield. Until that pressure eases or stocks stabilise, $3,400 is likely to remain the level traders watch. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6604 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia's 12% investment surge, the biggest since 2011, keeps RBA hike risk alive: Citi
item.description:
A stronger-than-expected capex print pushes back against the view that the RBA has finished tightening, which should support short-dated Australian government bond yields. It could also give the Australian dollar some support through its rate advantage, though global risk sentiment is likely to remain the bigger driver for the currency. Markets will look to the GDP release, along with the next inflation and labour market data, to judge whether the investment surge is feeding through to prices. A weakening jobs market would argue for a hold, while sticky inflation would strengthen the case for another hike, leaving the RBA's next move closely balanced.

---

An AI-fuelled surge in business investment has pushed Australian demand beyond what the economy can comfortably supply, and Citigroup warns that the RBA, while likely on hold for now, cannot rule out more hikes.

Summary:

  • Australian private business investment rose 12% q/q in the third quarter, the biggest gain since the 2011 mining boom, against a 4.3% consensus
  • Spending on equipment, plant and machinery jumped 23%, driven by AI-related investment
  • Domestic demand may have grown by as much as 1.5% in the quarter, lifting annual growth to around 3.3%
  • Citigroup says demand is now growing faster than the economy's potential, while the AI boom competes for land, labour and capital
  • Citi expects the RBA to keep the cash rate at 4.85%, but sees a risk of further rate hikes

Australian business investment posted its biggest quarterly jump in 15 years in the third quarter, and Citigroup warns that the economy is now running too hot for the Reserve Bank of Australia to rule out further rate hikes.

Private business investment rose 12% from the previous quarter, the largest gain since the mining boom of 2011 and almost three times the consensus forecast of around 4%. Spending on equipment, plant and machinery did the heavy lifting, surging 23% on the back of strong AI-related investment.

Citigroup chief economist Josh Williamson said domestic demand may have grown by as much as 1.5% in the quarter, lifting annual economic growth to around 3.3%, a pace he describes as overheated. In his view, demand is now growing faster than the economy's potential growth rate, the speed at which it can expand without generating extra inflation. At the same time, the AI investment boom is competing with the rest of the economy for land, labour and capital, adding to pressure on resources that are already stretched.

That combination matters for monetary policy. When demand persistently outruns the economy's capacity to supply, prices tend to rise, which is the risk central banks try to head off. Williamson's base case is that the RBA will keep the cash rate on hold at 4.85%, but he sees a real risk that the bank will have to tighten further.

The investment surge also changes the shape of the growth story. A boom led by equipment and technology spending can lift the economy's productive capacity over time, which would eventually ease inflation pressure. In the near term, though, the build-out itself adds to demand for workers, materials and finance, putting it in direct competition with households and other businesses.

The data will feed into the debate over how close the RBA is to the end of its tightening cycle. For markets, the key question is whether strong investment proves a one-off burst tied to AI projects or the start of a sustained upswing in capital spending. A sustained upswing would make a prolonged hold harder to defend and keep the door open to further hikes. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: OCBC sees the Indian rupee strengthening to 92.10 per dollar by end-2027 as oil relief builds
item.description:
For the rupee, oil is the swing factor. With OCBC keeping its end-2026 Brent forecast at $100 a barrel, any fresh attack on Gulf energy infrastructure or disruption around Hormuz could quickly reverse recent gains, since India imports most of its crude. The RBI's measures make one-way bets against the currency more expensive, which should limit sharp swings in USD/INR in either direction. A firm decision on India's inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index would be the clearest upside catalyst, as it would bring passive bond inflows. RBI reserve rebuilding means rupee strength is likely to be gradual, which suits carry trades more than outright momentum bets.

After a punishing year of oil shocks and outflows, the rupee has found its footing on RBI measures, cheaper crude and returning equity money, and OCBC expects gradual gains into 2027 as the central bank rebuilds its reserves.

---

Earlier:

  • Indian Rupee strengthens as falling oil prices ease pressure; Middle East escalation and recession trade remain key risks

---

Summary:

  • OCBC forecasts USD/INR at 92.10 by end-2027, pointing to a gradual rupee recovery
  • The rupee has held up since early November despite a broader emerging market currency selloff, with USD/INR below 94
  • RBI measures, including a 20% cash reserve requirement on certain FX derivatives, tighter NDF rules and a dollar window for state oil companies, curbed one-way pressure
  • Lower oil prices and recovering equity inflows, helped by rotation away from AI-heavy markets, have supported the currency
  • Oil remains a near-term risk, with OCBC keeping its end-2026 Brent forecast at $100 a barrel
  • Possible inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index could boost bond inflows, while RBI reserve rebuilding should slow gains

The Indian rupee is showing signs of a turnaround after a bruising year, and OCBC expects the recovery to extend into 2027 as oil prices ease and foreign money returns. The bank forecasts the dollar at 92.10 rupees by the end of next year, though it expects the Reserve Bank of India to slow the pace of gains by rebuilding its reserves.

The rupee spent much of 2026 under pressure from an oil price shock and persistent capital outflows. Since early November, however, it has held up well, even as a broader emerging market currency selloff took hold on worries about AI-driven growth and the risk of further Federal Reserve hikes, OCBC said in its daily market outlook. The dollar has traded below 94 rupees since early November.

Policy has done some of the work. The RBI introduced a 20% cash reserve requirement on certain foreign exchange derivatives and tightened rules on non-deliverable forwards, making it more expensive to hedge against rupee weakness. It also opened a special dollar window for state-owned oil companies. Together, those steps helped break the one-way pressure on the currency.

The backdrop has since turned more supportive. Lower oil prices have eased the strain on India's import bill, and equity inflows have recovered, helped by investors rotating away from markets heavily exposed to AI.

Oil remains the main near-term risk. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and renewed disruption around the Strait of Hormuz have revived supply concerns and could trigger rebounds in crude. OCBC is sticking with its end-2026 Brent forecast of $100 a barrel, as it sees limited prospects for a near-term negotiated settlement with Iran.

The bank expects more relief next year. It sees better prospects for de-escalation and additional export capacity in the Gulf bringing oil prices lower over 2027. That would improve India's terms of trade and reduce dollar demand from oil importers, giving the rupee a more lasting tailwind.

Bond flows could add a further boost. India's possible inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index is still under review and far from certain. If it happens, though, it could significantly widen foreign demand for Indian government bonds.

OCBC cautions that the road to a stronger rupee is unlikely to be smooth. After an extended period of intervention to defend the currency, the RBI is likely to use bouts of rupee strength to rebuild its foreign exchange reserves. That should slow the recovery rather than derail it.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman says hyperscalers can easily earn 15% on AI, but neoclouds face a utilisation trap
item.description:
The views point to a widening gap in how investors treat the AI trade. Hyperscaler stocks and investment-grade bonds look the most defensible, given their strong balance sheets and cash flows outside AI. Neocloud equity and high-yield credit carry the most risk if utilisation disappoints. Goldman's credit team expects the high-yield market for AI deals to split more sharply, with investors favouring top-tier developers and projects backed by solid contracts. Chipmakers and memory suppliers ultimately depend on the same thing as the neoclouds: evidence that companies using AI are earning a return. The next earnings round's commentary on returns on capital is likely to move the whole complex.

--

Goldman's analysis suggests the tech giants can comfortably earn a return on their AI build-out, but the neoclouds renting out GPU capacity are exposed if corporate customers keep failing to turn AI spending into profit.

Summary:

  • Goldman's Eric Sheridan estimates the six largest US hyperscalers can easily earn a return on invested capital of 15% or more on AI spending
  • Hyperscaler revenue backlogs have grown sharply, and only part of them needs to convert to revenue to reach that return
  • Social Capital's Chamath Palihapitiya warns that neoclouds have short-term revenue but long-dated, fixed obligations
  • Big companies are not yet seeing returns from AI that show up in earnings, which caps demand for computing power
  • Hyperscalers need around $1.4 trillion in cumulative revenue over 2028 to 2030 to earn 15% on their 2026 and 2027 investment
  • Weaker demand, tighter access to capital or a shortage of power could stall the investment cycle

Is the artificial intelligence spending boom built to last? Goldman Sachs put that question to two people who see the cycle from very different vantage points, and their answers point the same way. The biggest technology companies are well placed to ride out a slowdown. The risk is concentrated among newer, more heavily indebted players further down the chain.

Goldman's lead US internet analyst, Eric Sheridan, argued in the bank's November Top of Mind report that the six largest US hyperscalers can "very easily" earn a return on invested capital of 15% or more on their AI spending. Their revenue backlogs are much larger than two or three years ago, and some companies have said about half of those backlogs will turn into revenue within two years. On Goldman's estimates, the hyperscalers would not need anywhere near all of that backlog to convert to reach the 15% mark. Sheridan pointed to the latest earnings round, in which several of the big names gave detailed return figures and their shares rallied, as evidence that the payoff is starting to show.

He described the market's current doubts as understandable, rather than either warranted or overblown. Every computing cycle he has covered, from desktop to mobile to cloud, has gone through a phase of disillusionment once spending runs ahead of visible returns. Investors, he said, want returns within months on a build-out that typically plays out over five to eight years.

Chamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of Social Capital, invests across AI chips, power and software. He is more worried about the neoclouds, the specialist firms that rent out GPU capacity. He compares them to a bank in reverse: their revenue is short-term and uncertain, while their obligations for chips, power and data centres are long-dated and fixed. Like airlines, they need to keep their capacity busy to make money. He puts the break-even point at roughly 70% to 75% utilisation, with profits only coming above that. Yearly chip upgrades and more efficient AI models make the arithmetic harder.

His central concern is that big companies are not yet earning a meaningful return on their AI spending. Projects are hard to implement, staff are often wary, and productivity gains tend to get lost elsewhere in the business, so few firms can point to AI as a source of earnings growth. If that remains the case, demand for computing power may not grow fast enough to fill the capacity being built.

Goldman's analysts put the hurdle in numbers. For the hyperscalers to earn a 15% return on their 2026 and 2027 investment, they would need to generate around $1.4 trillion in cumulative revenue over 2028 to 2030, roughly $500 billion a year. Sheridan sees three things that could stall the cycle: weaker demand, a disruption in access to capital, or a shortage of power, which cannot be scaled up as fast as land, buildings or chips. For now, he sees demand gaining momentum rather than fading.

Both expect the cycle to produce winners and losers. Palihapitiya expects a bump in the road at some point, much like the internet build-out two decades ago, which ultimately proved right but got the timing wrong. Neoclouds that own their power and land should hold up better than those that simply lease capacity.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test
item.description:
Gold's moves are being set by the dollar and US rate pricing, not by safe-haven demand, so US data and Fed commentary will matter more than geopolitical headlines for any rebound. Because speculative positioning has been cut so hard, short covering could make any bounce sharp, especially in silver, the most stretched metal. A failure back below Wednesday's low would suggest forced selling has further to run. That would be a risk for miners and leveraged exposure. A softer dollar or a dovish shift in Fed expectations is the catalyst most likely to turn a technical rebound into a lasting one.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold remains caught between forced liquidations and hawkish Fed bets. What could trigger a reversal?
  • Gold claws back $160 from a 14-month low, but one candle doesn't necessarily make a bottom

---

Gold has gone from historic exuberance to historic distress in less than a year, and while stretched positioning and a strong seasonal record point to a bounce, Saxo's Ole Hansen says a lasting recovery needs the dollar and rate expectations to ease.

Summary:

  • Gold has swung from about 45% above its 200-day moving average in January to about 20% below, the deepest gap since 2013
  • Gold is down about 19% this year and around 37% from its record high, its biggest 12-month drawdown since the early 1980s
  • Silver is down about 43% this year and platinum about 39%, with silver more than 37% below its long-term trend
  • Oversold momentum, reduced speculative positioning and a strong December–January track record favour a short-term rebound
  • A daily gold close above about $3,590 would confirm a rebound toward $3,700, while a break below Wednesday's low would cancel it
  • A lasting recovery depends on a softer dollar, lower real yields, easing inflation and steadier stock markets

Gold's selloff has swung from one historic extreme to another, and Saxo's head of commodity strategy, Ole Hansen, now sees early signs that the selling may be running out of steam. He cautions that any lasting recovery still depends on the macro backdrop turning in the metal's favour.

In January, gold traded about 45% above its 200-day moving average, the widest gap since the 1970s. This week it slipped about 20% below that average, the deepest negative gap since June 2013, Hansen wrote in a note published by Saxo. That compares with roughly 20% below during the 2008 financial crisis and about 27% below in 1981. Gold is down about 19% this year and around 37% from January's record high, its biggest 12-month drawdown since the early 1980s. The rest of the sector has fared worse. Silver has fallen about 43% this year and sits more than 37% below its 200-day average. Platinum is down about 39%, and palladium is around a third below its trend.

Hansen blames a broad move out of risk rather than a collapse in gold's longer-term case. A strong dollar, energy-driven inflation, rising expectations of rate hikes, turmoil in AI-linked stocks and negative momentum have all pushed investors to raise cash. Higher rate expectations also make it more expensive to hold metals that pay no yield. He argues the long-term supports remain in place, including central banks diversifying their reserves, fiscal worries and demand for assets without counterparty risk. But he says these alone are unlikely to stop the selling.

The setup for a rebound is improving. Short-term momentum readings across the sector are at or below oversold levels, and speculative positioning has been cut substantially. Gold ETF holdings have held up relatively well, and silver has drawn fresh ETF demand despite falling prices. Seasonality also helps: gold has gained over December and January in each of the past 11 years. Hansen stresses that neither oversold conditions nor the calendar is a reason to buy on its own.

He sets out clear technical markers. Gold formed a hammer candle at its recent low near $3,430, a pattern that can signal selling exhaustion. A daily close above about $3,590 would confirm a rebound and open the way to around $3,700, a 38.2% retracement of the November selloff. A fresh break below Wednesday's low would cancel that view. For silver, a daily close above roughly $41.50 would be the equivalent confirmation.

Hansen is also less convinced than markets that the Federal Reserve needs to deliver the rate hikes now priced in. He argues that weaker AI investment, falling diesel prices and a negative wealth effect from lower stock prices could cool inflation and change the Fed's course. A rally driven by short covering could come quickly. A durable recovery, though, would need a softer dollar, lower real yields and calmer stock markets, which he says would not require a renewed AI boom. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ECB picks Spain's Hernández de Cos as president, with 3 tests waiting from day one
item.description:
For bonds, the appointment matters most for the gap between French and German yields. Markets may treat a president who backed quantitative easing as a slightly firmer safety net for French debt, but his record on fiscal discipline makes a blanket rescue unlikely. That leaves French spreads tied to the election campaign more than to the ECB. The euro's immediate reaction is likely to be muted, since Hernández de Cos is seen as a continuity candidate, not someone who will change the direction of rates. Brunnermeier as chief economist is worth watching, as his academic work on financial stability could shape how the bank thinks about stepping into markets.

---

Earlier heads up on this:

  • EU leaders set to confirm backing for Spain's De Cos as next ECB President - report

---

Europe has handed the ECB to a soft-spoken Spanish technocrat who backed quantitative easing but preaches fiscal discipline, and France's shaky bond market and looming election may test which instinct wins within weeks of his arrival.

Summary:

  • EU leaders chose Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down in February
  • The European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council still need to endorse him, with final EU approval expected in December
  • He will be the ECB's first Spanish president and currently heads the Bank for International Settlements
  • He beat Dutch central banker Klaas Knot, seen as the more conservative candidate
  • France's volatile bond market and a presidential election two months into his term are likely to be the first tests
  • Germany's Markus Brunnermeier and France's Laurence Boone are expected to join the ECB's Executive Board
  • Info via Wall Street Journal (gated) 

European leaders have chosen Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank. They are betting that a soft-spoken technocrat can steer the euro area through French debt worries, weak growth and nervous stock markets. He will be the first Spaniard to run the ECB.

Hernández de Cos, 55, will succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down in February, according to The Wall Street Journal. The nomination still needs endorsements from the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, with EU leaders expected to give final approval in December. He beat Dutch central banker Klaas Knot, the only other contender. Knot was seen as the more conservative candidate and had spent recent months trying to shed that image.

He is a career central banker. He began as an economist at the Bank of Spain, rose to become its governor, and now heads the Bank for International Settlements, which serves as a bank for the world's central banks. Former colleagues describe him as quiet but technically formidable, with expertise ranging from fiscal policy to stablecoins. His former doctoral supervisor, who later brought him to Frankfurt as an adviser at the ECB, remembers a skilled networker and a tough debating partner on monetary policy.

His first big test is likely to come from France. The French bond market has become volatile amid concern about rising debt and political deadlock, and Hernández de Cos will take office two months before voting begins to choose Emmanuel Macron's successor. The two front-runners, Marine Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left, have both criticised the ECB and pressed it to help lower France's borrowing costs.

The ECB has tools to calm bond markets, but policymakers are likely to be reluctant to support a country whose problems are widely seen as self-inflicted. That leaves the new president in a delicate position. Hernández de Cos backed the quantitative easing programmes that helped heavily indebted countries, but he has also consistently argued for fiscal discipline. Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said the appointment would probably raise market expectations that the ECB would step in if conditions got very bad. But he cautioned investors against treating it as a reason to load up on French risk.

The choice also reflected the usual political balancing. Unwritten rules made it unlikely that Germany or France would win the top job: a German, Ursula von der Leyen, already leads the European Commission, and France was unlikely to land the presidency again straight after Lagarde. Both countries are instead set to take seats on the ECB's six-member Executive Board. Princeton professor Markus Brunnermeier is expected to become chief economist, while French economist Laurence Boone is in line to oversee market operations.

The next few months will show whether a quiet technocrat can balance market stability against fiscal discipline, especially if France's election pushes up its borrowing costs. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan sees bitcoin capitulation in record Strategy discount, but 3 risks cloud the call
item.description:
For bitcoin, the June closing low near $58,500 is now the key level. A clean break would put the next on-chain support clusters, around $57,000 and then $47,000, in play, and would probably trigger more selling from miners whose costs sit well above the price. For Strategy shareholders, forced selling by index funds around the November 30 MSCI removal could widen the discount further before any rebound. Heavy options positioning could make moves in either direction more violent. A recovery in the ratio back above 1, as happened in July, would be the clearest sign that sellers are finished.

---

Earlier:

  • Bitcoin consolidates at yearly lows as traders await fresh catalyst amid negative backdrop

---

JPMorgan reads Strategy's record discount to its bitcoin holdings as a sign that selling may be nearly exhausted, but ETF outflows, struggling miners and a looming index removal mean the market has yet to confirm a bottom.

Summary:

  • Strategy traded at 0.88 times its bitcoin holdings on Wednesday, a record low on JPMorgan's enterprise-value measure
  • The previous low of 0.89 came in late June, when bitcoin closed near $58,500, and the ratio recovered above 1 by early July
  • Strategy's removal from MSCI indexes on November 30 could force fund selling and distort the signal
  • Outflows from BlackRock's spot bitcoin ETF are running faster than during the May to June sell-off
  • JPMorgan puts bitcoin production costs at about $86,000, well above the current price near $60,500
  • Historical bottom indicators suggest the low may not be in yet

Strategy, the world's largest corporate holder of bitcoin, has fallen to a record discount to the value of its bitcoin holdings on JPMorgan's preferred measure. The bank's analysts see this as a possible sign that selling in the cryptocurrency is close to capitulation. Several other indicators suggest the bottom may not be in yet.

According to BeInCrypto, which reported the findings, the bank's Flows and Liquidity team calculates that the company formerly known as MicroStrategy was valued at 0.88 times its bitcoin holdings on Wednesday. The measure compares the bitcoin holdings with the company's enterprise value, which includes its debt and preferred stock as well as its equity. The previous low of 0.89 came in late June, when bitcoin posted a closing low of around $58,500. The ratio then recovered above 1 by early July. Strategy's own dashboard, which uses a different calculation, shows a reading of around 0.94.

Readings this deep tend to reflect extreme pessimism, and similar conditions have often appeared near market lows. There is a complication this time. Strategy is due to be removed from MSCI indexes on November 30, which will force index-tracking funds to sell the shares regardless of value. That could push the discount wider for technical rather than fundamental reasons. Speculative positioning is also unusually heavy. Executive chairman Michael Saylor says outstanding options on the stock equal about 61% of its market value, compared with around 14% for Tesla.

The flow picture remains difficult. JPMorgan notes that investors kept pulling money from BlackRock's spot bitcoin ETF even during a brief price rebound, and at a faster pace than in the May to June sell-off. Miners are under strain too. The bank puts the cost of producing one bitcoin at about $86,000, up from $85,000 in September, well above the current price near $60,500. Estimates based on MARA Holdings' filings put costs closer to $63,000, a level the price is now testing. Higher-cost producers may have to sell reserves to stay afloat.

Others are more cautious. One crypto research firm says only two of its 13 historical bottom signals had triggered as of November 22, and that after seven similar support breakdowns, the eventual low came at least 17% further down. The head of research at an on-chain analytics firm warned that bottoming and recovery have historically taken months, even with short-term rallies along the way.

On-chain cost-basis data points to resistance near $63,000, with around $57,000 seen as the critical threshold below the June low. Deeper support clusters sit near $47,000 and $38,000. For now, the June low near $58,500 is the line to watch. A record discount at Strategy suggests sellers may be close to exhausted, but the market has not yet confirmed a bottom.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Five questions over Nvidia's China chip trail that Huang's return has not settled
item.description:
For Nvidia shareholders, the main risk is regulatory rather than personal. Tougher know-your-customer enforcement, or a revival of the push to require location tracking on chips, could slow shipments into Southeast Asia, which has been one of the company's biggest billing hubs. The stock already lost a large amount of market value during (well, prior to) the leadership crisis, so any new enforcement action or congressional hearing could hit sentiment quickly. Server makers such as Super Micro Computer are also exposed because of the pending prosecution. More broadly, the case adds to US-China tech tensions at a time when Washington's chip export policy is already in flux.

---

Earlier:

  • My Nvidia stock analysis shows bulls are better than what most seem to think

---

Jensen Huang is back in charge at Nvidia, but a pointed column argues that the company's public statements on chip smuggling, customer checks and Singapore revenue still don't line up with what has emerged in court filings and official probes.

Summary:

  • A National Review opinion column argues Nvidia's public statements on AI chip diversion to China are inconsistent with the evidence
  • US prosecutors have charged a Super Micro Computer executive and two others over the alleged diversion of Nvidia-equipped servers to China
  • US authorities are running a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer that Nvidia blocked in June 2025
  • The column questions Huang's 2025 "no evidence" remarks and a change in how Nvidia reported its Singapore revenue
  • Nvidia says earlier diversion allegations were investigated and unfounded, and Megaspeed denies wrongdoing
  • Huang resigned on November 12 and was reinstated by the board on November 23

I came across this and it raises some interesting questions, so I thought I'd share. A column in National Review (may be gated) this week sets out, point by point, why it believes Nvidia's public account of how its restricted AI chips reached China doesn't hold together. It argues the gaps remain even after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as chief executive and the president's statement that the Justice Department has no evidence of unlawful conduct by him.

The column starts from what is already on the record. Federal prosecutors in New York have charged a senior Super Micro Computer executive, a Taiwan-based sales manager and a contractor over an alleged scheme to divert servers built with Nvidia GPUs to buyers in China. The indictment alleges that more than $500 million of those servers were diverted in a matter of weeks in the spring of 2025. Separately, US authorities confirmed this month that they are pursuing a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, over possible export control violations. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list in June 2025.

Against that background, the column revisits Huang's May 2025 remark that there was "no evidence of any AI chip diversion," along with his argument that the systems were too heavy to smuggle. It points out that Singapore had already publicly disclosed a probe into servers fitted with Nvidia chips by then, and that Nvidia was marketing a desktop-sized Grace Blackwell machine at the time. It also questions a change in Nvidia's regulatory filings in late 2025, when Singapore stopped being reported as a separate revenue region shortly after the company blocked Megaspeed. The columnist sees the timing as convenient. Nvidia's filing said the change came from a switch to reporting revenue by the location of customers' headquarters rather than their billing address.

Other strands come from lawmakers. In March, Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote jointly to the Commerce Secretary. They argued that the evidence of diversion was public at the time and that companies can't avoid their know-your-customer obligations by not looking. Representative Bill Foster has said Nvidia staff told him privately that tracking where chips end up was technically feasible, even as the industry's trade group publicly called such requirements untested.

Nvidia's position is that the earlier diversion allegations involving Megaspeed were investigated and found to be unfounded, and Megaspeed says several inspections found no wrongdoing. Huang stepped down on November 12 after admitting infidelity, amid reports of a relationship with a former Megaspeed executive. The board reinstated him on November 23, saying it was satisfied with his candour. The Justice Department has said it hasn't concluded whether that executive was working for Chinese intelligence.

None of this shows that Huang or Nvidia broke the law, and the column is an opinion piece. But regulators, lawmakers and shareholders are likely to keep asking the questions it raises about export controls, customer checks and disclosure. For investors, the risk is less about one executive and more about whether tighter enforcement or chip-tracking rules could slow Nvidia's sales into Asia.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears
item.description:
Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement.

---

Cheaper fuel has pushed Kiwi consumer confidence back above 100 and pulled inflation expectations to a 22-month low, but households still feel better about the future than the present and remain wary of big purchases.

Summary:

  • Consumer confidence rose 4 points to 100.2 in November, the highest since January but still below the long-run average of 112
  • The future conditions index rose to around 111 and the current conditions index to around 84
  • Two-year inflation expectations fell to 3.9% from 4.2%, the lowest since January 2025 and well down from April's 6.6%
  • The 12-month economic outlook improved to a net 6% pessimistic, while the five-year outlook rose to a net 16% optimistic
  • A net 12% still see it as a bad time to buy major household items, a 6-point improvement
  • House price expectations rose to 2.3% from 2.0%, still below the 3.5% average

New Zealand consumer confidence climbed back above the 100 mark in November. Falling fuel prices pulled households' inflation expectations to their lowest level in nearly two years, and both the current and future measures of sentiment improved.

The ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence index rose 4 points to 100.2, its strongest reading since January, according to the survey released on Friday. That is still well short of the long-run average of 112, so the recovery from April's low near 80 is not complete. Both components improved. The future conditions index rose to around 111 from 106, while the current conditions index edged up to around 84 from 81.

The biggest shift came in inflation expectations. Households now see prices rising 3.9% a year over the next two years, down from 4.2% in October and the lowest since January 2025. That is a steep fall from April's 6.6%, when a spike in pump prices pushed expectations sharply higher. The survey's authors noted that consumers' price expectations fell slightly more than fuel prices over the month, after tracking them almost one-for-one earlier in the year. They also pointed out that inflation expectations and confidence have moved in opposite directions in recent years, which suggests the two are linked.

The economic outlook improved but stayed gloomy for the next 12 months. A net 6% of respondents expect bad times for the economy over that period, compared with a net 13% a month earlier. The five-year view rose to a net 16% positive from 8%, close to its long-run average of 19%. Views on household finances were mixed. A net 20% said they were worse off than a year ago, a marginal improvement. A net 22% expect to be better off a year from now, down from 24% but far above April's low of 3%.

Appetite for spending remains soft. A net 12% still think it is a bad time to buy a major household item, although that is a 6-point improvement on October. House price expectations rose to 2.3% from 2.0%, still well below the survey's 3.5% average.

The survey's authors described the overall mood as below par, citing broader cost-of-living pressures and a soft labour market. They cautioned that consumers' inflation expectations carry less weight for monetary policy than those of businesses, which actually set prices. Households feel better about the future than about the present, which suggests they are not yet ready to spend freely. The next survey is due on December 18. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tokyo CPI preview: core inflation seen jumping to 3% three weeks before BoJ decision
item.description:
A firm Tokyo print would add support for the yen, which is still trading near 160 per dollar despite close to $100 billion of intervention. The Fed is also hiking, so the rate gap stays wide, and a BoJ hike on its own may not change the yen's direction much without signs of a quicker pace afterwards. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields are the most exposed if the core-core measure meets or beats forecast. A miss would likely weigh on the yen and could revive talk of the BoJ pausing, especially if Nikkei weakness continues.

---

Tokyo inflation is expected to rise to around 3% on both core gauges today, giving markets their last clean read on price pressure before a Bank of Japan meeting widely tipped to deliver a third hike of 2026.

Summary:

  • Tokyo November CPI is due at 23:30 GMT on Thursday (18:30 US Eastern), Friday morning in Tokyo
  • Core CPI (ex fresh food) is expected at 3.0%, up from 2.6%; the ex fresh food and energy measure is also seen at 3.0%, up from 2.4%
  • Headline Tokyo CPI was 2.8% in October; no consensus is listed for November
  • Tokyo data is an imperfect but useful lead for nationwide CPI, which is due 23:30 GMT on December 17, hours before the BoJ decision
  • Most economists expect the BoJ to hike to 1.50% from 1.25% at its December 17 to 18 meeting
  • A hawkish board member has flagged upside inflation risks from the Middle East war, the weak yen and AI-related demand

Main article: Tokyo's November consumer price data, due at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern) on Thursday, Friday morning in Japan, is expected to show a sharp pickup in inflation in the capital. It arrives three weeks before a Bank of Japan meeting at which a rate hike is widely expected.

Consensus looks for core Tokyo CPI, which strips out fresh food, to jump to 3.0% from 2.6% in October. The measure that excludes both fresh food and energy is also forecast at 3.0%, up from 2.4%. The BoJ watches that measure more closely as a guide to underlying, demand-driven price pressure. Headline Tokyo inflation ran at 2.8% in October. If the forecasts are met, every key gauge would sit well above the central bank's 2% target.

The Tokyo figures matter because they come out roughly three weeks before the nationwide numbers. They are an imperfect guide: spending in the capital differs from the rest of the country, and nationwide core inflation was only around 2.2% in October. Still, the direction usually carries over. The timing gives the Tokyo release extra weight this month. The nationwide November data is not due until 23:30 GMT on December 17 (18:30 US Eastern). That is the morning of December 18 in Tokyo, the second and final day of the BoJ's December 17 to 18 meeting, so the national data will land only hours before the policy announcement and too late to shape much of the debate. Today's numbers are effectively the last major inflation reading markets can absorb before the decision.

Expectations for that meeting are firm. A Reuters poll published last week found 86% of economists expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.50% from 1.25%. That would make 2026 Japan's first year with three hikes since the late 1980s. Nearly 60% of respondents expect a further rise to 1.75% by the end of March. Market pricing has been a little more cautious, implying odds of a December move of roughly 75% to 80%.

The hawkish case has also gained support from inside the bank. Board member Naoki Tamura said this week that the BoJ should respond quickly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by raising rates faster. In his view, the Middle East war, higher import costs from the weak yen and strong demand for AI-related goods all pose upside risks to prices, and the policy rate is still some way below neutral.

There are risks to a hike. Japan's economy shrank in the July to September quarter, and a sharp slide in the Nikkei this month has raised questions about whether the bank might pause. Most economists in the Reuters poll said stock market volatility would not stop a December hike, though a prolonged selloff remains the main risk to that view.

A reading at or above forecast would strengthen the case for a hike. A soft reading, especially in the measure that excludes fresh food and energy, would give the bank's more cautious members something to point to. Even so, one miss is unlikely to overturn a move that policymakers have been preparing markets for.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: CoreWeave bond yields are approaching 19%. Why even stock investors should pay attention
item.description:
The AI infrastructure boom requires enormous amounts of capital

CoreWeave's falling bond prices offer a warning about the financial risks behind that expansion, even as demand for AI computing continues to grow.

Investors following CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) may want to look beyond its stock chart. On November 25, the yield on one of the company's bonds reached 17.91%, while another traded at a record-low price consistent with a yield of approximately 18.6%.

For shareholders, this is a development worth understanding as the stock is not too far from its all time low, apx 9% above its IPO opening price and still over 77% below its all time high

What are bonds, and why do their yields rise?

When a company issues a bond, it is essentially borrowing money from investors. In return, it promises to pay interest and repay the principal according to agreed terms.

Let's take CoreWeave's 9.75% bond, due in October 2031, as an example.

  • Face value: $1,000

  • Annual interest payments: $97.50

  • Market price on November 25: $742.30

  • Reported yield to maturity: 17.91%

Someone purchasing the bond at that price would pay $742.30 for a security scheduled to repay $1,000 at maturity, while also receiving interest payments along the way.

Assuming CoreWeave meets all its payment obligations, the discounted purchase price helps explain the considerably higher annualized yield.

But why would existing investors sell such a bond at a steep discount?

They may be concerned about the company's ability to repay its debt, require greater compensation for taking that risk, or prefer to reduce their exposure altogether.

When bond prices fall, their yields rise. An exceptionally high corporate bond yield is often a warning rather than a bargain.

CoreWeave is growing rapidly. So are its financing needs.

CoreWeave provides the computing infrastructure that companies use to develop and operate artificial intelligence applications. Building that infrastructure requires expensive chips, data centers, electricity and substantial upfront investment.

Its third-quarter financial results illustrate the financial challenge:

  • Quarterly revenue: $3.66 billion, up approximately 168% year over year.

  • Quarterly net interest expense: $846 million.

  • Quarterly net loss: $709 million.

  • Expected 2026 capital expenditure: $37 billion to $39 billion.

  • Expected fourth-quarter interest expense: $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion.

The company is generating considerably more revenue than a year ago. Yet financing its expansion remains expensive.

A company can experience tremendous demand for its products and still face financial difficulties if the cost of delivering those products and servicing its debt is too high.

Does CoreWeave now have to borrow at 18%?

Not necessarily.

The rising market yield does not automatically change the interest rate CoreWeave pays on its existing fixed-rate bonds. It does, however, suggest that raising new comparable unsecured debt could become considerably more expensive.

Consider a hypothetical company borrowing $1 billion at different interest rates:

The difference between borrowing at 7% and 18% would be $110 million in additional annual interest expenses.

Interestingly, Bloomberg reported on November 25 that CoreWeave's banks are preparing a $4.5 billion loan tied to its business with Meta Platforms. Preliminary pricing discussions reportedly center on 7%-7.5%, although the transaction has yet to be finalized.

The financing benefits from specific assets and a major customer contract, making its risk profile different from CoreWeave's unsecured corporate bonds.

This is a useful reminder that even a financially pressured company can have access to more attractive financing under certain conditions.

Why Nvidia and Nasdaq traders should care

CoreWeave is part of a much larger AI investment cycle.

Companies borrow money, purchase graphics processing units (GPUs), construct data centers and sell computing capacity to customers developing AI applications.

If financing becomes increasingly expensive across the industry, some companies may need to slow their expansion, postpone equipment purchases or raise additional equity from shareholders.

That could eventually affect chip manufacturers such as Nvidia (NVDA), data center operators and other businesses benefiting from AI infrastructure spending.

It does not mean that AI demand is disappearing. It raises a different question: how profitable and financially sustainable will meeting that demand be?

What stock traders should watch next

CoreWeave's bond prices could offer useful additional context when evaluating a recovery in its shares.

If CRWV stock rebounds while its bonds remain under considerable pressure, credit investors may still have reservations about the company's financial position.

A recovery in both the stock and bond prices would offer more encouraging evidence, particularly if accompanied by successful financing transactions.

The proposed Meta-related loan is another development worth following. Its final interest rate, size and investor demand could help reveal whether lenders are still comfortable financing substantial AI infrastructure projects when additional protections are available.

You don't need to trade bonds to benefit from watching them. The corporate bond market offers another perspective on the financial health of the companies whose shares you trade.

What else I'm watching: Is the stock market recovery gaining credibility?

While CoreWeave's bond market is sending a warning, other parts of the financial markets are showing early signs of improvement. The contrast is worth following.

Our latest investingLive earnings sentiment research shows that selling pressure following corporate earnings may be easing, particularly among larger companies. However, the recovery is still relatively narrow, with fewer than 40% of Wednesday's earnings reporters posting positive stock reactions.

There are encouraging developments overseas, too. As Justin Low reports, European stocks are rallying following Wall Street's remarkable turnaround. The bigger test will come next week, when US investors return from Thanksgiving and market liquidity normalizes.

Within the AI sector itself, my latest Nvidia stock analysis identifies several constructive technical developments. Nvidia has broken out of its descending channel and demonstrated some relative strength against Nasdaq futures. Reclaiming the $155 to $155.50 area would further strengthen its recovery case.

There is also an interesting historical perspective. As Eamonn Sheridan reports, Citi's research shows that the S&P 500 was higher six months later in 13 of the previous 14 instances when the VIX reached 40. Extreme fear has often presented opportunities for patient investors, although history offers no guarantees.

What I would particularly like to see is whether improving equity market sentiment is accompanied by an improvement in corporate bond prices.

If technology stocks continue recovering while the debt financing their expansion remains under severe pressure, I would treat the rally with some caution. A recovery in both markets would make a more convincing case that investors are regaining confidence in the AI investment cycle.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: EU leaders set to confirm backing for Spain's De Cos as next ECB President - report
item.description:
Reuters reports, citing EU diplomats, that EU leaders are set to sign off on Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank.

This has been well telegraphed. Christine Lagarde is leaving early. She steps down on February 7, nine months before her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027. The timing is political. Leaving early lets EU leaders lock in a successor before April's French presidential election, where polls favour Marine Le Pen (and will be a major event in FX markets next year).

The race was really decided when Paris and Berlin agreed on a deal. France backed De Cos for the top job and proposed a Frenchwoman for the market operations role. That left Germany free to nominate the chief economist, and Berlin wants that seat for Princeton professor Markus Brunnermeier. The deal squeezed out Klaas Knot. Dutch media reported last week that he's expected to withdraw. The formal sign-off is aimed at the December 17-18 summit.

In terms of policy, De Cos was seen as slightly more dovish than Knot. More important is the backstop angle. He's a southern European and a Draghi ally, which reinforces the view that Frankfurt will step in if spreads blow out, whether that's true or not. T

There's nothing here for EUR/USD today. It's priced, and the ECB is a committee. Still, at the margin it's a mild dovish tilt and a vote for tighter BTP and OAT spreads into 2027. The next thing to watch is who gets the chief economist job. With Brunnermeier as the German pick, the hawks would keep a strong voice on the Executive Board and we're back to the typical dovish tilt at the ECB with the hawkish criticism coming from the Germans.

Today, the euro is up 14 pips to 1.0985.

item.title: Wall Street’s earnings mood is starting to improve. Is the stock market finding a bottom?
item.description:
Wall Street’s earnings mood is starting to improve. Is the stock market finding a bottom?

Exclusive investingLive research reveals early signs of recovery in post-earnings stock performance. Meanwhile, hedge funds have increased their short exposure, potentially setting the stage for a sharper rebound if market conditions stabilize.

November 26, 2026

Wall Street is showing signs that the selling pressure of recent weeks may be losing some of its effectiveness. Our latest earnings sentiment research, Wednesday's remarkable stock market recovery and the subsequent rally in European equities provide reasons for cautious optimism. But underneath the surface, plenty of stocks are still struggling.

investingLive Earnings Mood: 4.5 out of 10

Our proprietary earnings research shows an interesting discrepancy between how larger companies and the average stock are reacting to quarterly results.

Wednesday's average stock reaction, giving every company equal importance regardless of its size, was actually negative 4%

Deere gained approximately 4.4%, while HP jumped 11.5%. Excluding just these two companies would turn Wednesday's capitalization-weighted earnings reaction from positive 1.73% to negative 0.50%.

That is a fairly concentrated recovery.

Dell stock offers an encouraging clue

Dell Technologies (DELL) is one of the more interesting stocks to examine following Wednesday's trading session.

After reporting earnings on Tuesday evening, Dell fell more than 10% from its pre-earnings closing price before recovering the entire decline.

The initial selling was effectively rejected. For investors looking to identify a potential change in market sentiment, these failed selloffs can be particularly informative.

Dick's Sporting Goods and Abercrombie & Fitch also extended their initial earnings gains, bringing their cumulative advances to approximately 18.6% and 26%, respectively.

There are less encouraging examples, of course. Nutanix, Ambarella and Urban Outfitters suffered double-digit earnings declines.

Nasdaq and S&P 500 futures are showing early signs of stabilization

Wednesday's selloff presented bears with an opportunity to establish fresh lows below those recorded last Friday. Neither of the two major equity futures markets did so.

Both markets have recovered approximately 5% from their November 20 lows.

For traders, two upside references are particularly interesting:

  • Nasdaq futures: 27,137, Monday's high.
  • S&P 500 futures: 7,313.25, Monday's high.

Reclaiming and sustaining prices above these levels would strengthen the recovery case. Conversely, breaking last Friday's lows would undermine it considerably.

European markets are also participating in the relief rally, with the Euro Stoxx gaining 1.8% and Germany's DAX rising 1.6% at Thursday's opening, as Justin Low reported in his European stock market update.

Hedge funds are positioned for trouble. Could that help the bulls?

According to Goldman Sachs, hedge fund clients reduced their exposure for five consecutive weeks before aggressively increasing their short positions.

As Eamonn Sheridan reported, ETF short exposure recorded its third-largest weekly increase in a decade.

Such positioning creates an interesting possibility. If stocks continue stabilizing, some short sellers may begin buying back shares to close their positions, while other fund managers may gradually increase their market exposure.

That could accelerate a recovery. It does not necessarily require a major improvement in corporate fundamentals to get started, although sustained gains would need broader support.

Nvidia remains central to the recovery

Earlier today, our Nvidia stock analysis identified several encouraging technical developments, including its rebound from $141.17 and a break above its descending price channel.

The fundamental picture is more complicated.

S&P has placed Nvidia’s AA credit rating on negative watch, while Moody’s has maintained its Aa1 rating and stable outlook. Both have raised concerns surrounding governance and dependence on Jensen Huang.

Nvidia's ability to sustain its recovery despite these lingering concerns could provide another indication of whether investors are becoming more comfortable taking risk again.

What stock market investors should watch next

Three developments would make the bullish case more convincing:

  • More companies attracting buyers after earnings, rather than a handful of influential stocks supporting the averages.
  • Recent earnings winners retaining their gains and more initial selloffs reversing, as Dell's did.
  • Nasdaq and S&P 500 futures establishing higher highs and higher lows.

With US stock exchanges closed for Thanksgiving and reopening for a shortened Friday session, next week should provide a better test of conviction.

There is enough evidence to start questioning the bearish narrative. There is not yet enough to declare that the correction is over.

item.title: Connecting the dots: Is big tech starting to outgrow its own valuation playbook?
item.description:
One of the things that Wall Street has always loved about big tech is its ability to make an obscene amount of money without having to spend an equally obscene amount of money to grow. Or at least that used to be how it used to be.

Historically, the appeal of software and digital platforms has always been their ability to scale. Selling another million software subscriptions doesn't necessarily require building another factory. As such, revenues can grow much faster than the cost of doing business. And that is part of the reason Wall Street has been so comfortable attaching lofty valuations to tech stocks. However, the AI trade is a completely different beast.

Between the need for data centres, expensive chips, electricity and networking infrastructure, growth is becoming a much more expensive affair.

And as investors are grappling with the latest selloff in tech stocks, perhaps we should be asking how big of an issue is the changing economics of the tech business itself? Let's try to put things into perspective.

According to a research published by Brookings, the combined capex by Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle is projected to exceed $800 billion this year. For some context, that figure was just a measly $97 billion back in 2020.

And what is even more striking is that their combined capital spending is projected to exceed the cash generated by their operations.

In July, an analysis by Reuters suggested that for every additional dollar of operating cash flow that these companies are expected to generate between 2025 and 2027, they will be increasing capital spending by roughly $1.57.

In simpler terms, it means that as the businesses grow, then so is the cost of delivering that growth.

So, what exactly does all of this mean for valuations?

Well, just imagine two companies generating $100 billion in operating cash flow. One needs to reinvest $20 billion, while the other needs to reinvest $80 billion. Would you be comfortable paying the same price for both, assuming that they hold similar future growth prospects? Bzzt. I certainly wouldn't.

And that's the point that investors seem to be waking up to in the last few months. If we're still valuing tech stocks primarily on revenue and earnings growth, we risk overlooking how much more expensive that growth is becoming. Capital spending takes a bite out of cash flow upfront, while depreciation will weigh on reported earnings for years to come.

To put things into a simpler question: Does a tech company growing its earnings by 20% today deserve the same valuation multiple as it did five years ago if it now needs to commit considerably more capital to deliver that same growth?

For me, that's where the traditional valuation playbook might need a bit of a rethink. Or perhaps we're already seeing that change in the way that investors have been reacting to even some of the blockbuster earnings beats on Wall Street as of late.

It used to be that beating earnings estimates and raising revenue guidance was pretty much the dream combination for tech stocks. These days, investors also want to know how much bigger the cheque is going to be to deliver on those promises.

As such, I reckon that free cash flow yields and returns on invested capital are going to feature much more prominently in the conversation going forward. In looking at the next phase, it might not necessarily be the fastest-growing tech companies that deserve the richest valuations anymore. Instead, it is those that can turn that growth into meaningful returns without constantly having to reach deeper into their pockets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
